summary:
No statute establishes a procedure for legal gender recognition in Latvia, and no targeted legislation on the question has been adopted. Reporting by the national public broadcaster in June 2025 quoted coalition members of parliament stating that trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet." One trans immigrant interviewed in the same feature said that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status, placing his residence permit at risk.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have been in force since 1 July 2024, having been codified in November 2023. They are not marriage. A 2006 constitutional amendment defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and same-sex couples cannot marry.

Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised. Male homosexuality was decriminalised in 1992 and female homosexuality was never criminalised; the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1999 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

The most serious institutional failure documented concerns hate-crime enforcement. In Hanovs v. Latvia, decided unanimously by the European Court of Human Rights on 18 July 2024, the Court found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 following a 2020 homophobic attack on a gay couple in Riga. No criminal charges were brought even though the aggressor admitted using anti-gay slurs, and the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter resolved with a lenient fine. The Court held that the failure to prosecute fostered impunity for hate-motivated offences.

Enforcement has moved after the judgment. The Prosecutor General reopened criminal proceedings in the Hanovs case. In a separate 2024 incident in which two people were attacked in Daugavpils, the Prosecutor General ordered the investigation reopened after police had closed it. Homophobic posts by a former member of the European Parliament were also placed under investigation; he left for Russia.

Protection machinery does function in some channels. An administrative court overturned a denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker. The Ombudsman had earlier called for a partnership law, and a 2020 court ruling in favour of parental leave rights for same-sex couples prompted a Justice Ministry draft civil union law in 2022.

No legal restriction on access to sex-segregated facilities is documented in the sources. Employment protection covers sexual orientation under Labour Code amendments passed in September 2006, but the sources describe no discrimination protection on the basis of gender identity. ILGA-Europe ranked Latvia 24th of 27 European Union countries for LGBT rights protection in 2023.
tangentialFactors:
Public visibility carries a mixed record. Around 8,000 people marched in Baltic Pride 2018 in Riga, an annual event rotating among Baltic capitals and organised by a local LGBTI group under the motto "See Diversity! See Freedom!" Latvia was the first European Union country to elect an openly gay head of state, in 2023. Against this, the Archbishop of Riga Cardinal Jānis Pujats called homosexuality "total corruption in the sexual arena" and "an unnatural form of prostitution" in 2007, demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage, and called for crowds of 40,000 to 50,000 to counter Pride, which he described as a "foreign-inspired action."

The organised gay scene is confined to the capital. Bars, clubs, stores and libraries established since democratisation are concentrated in Riga, and outside it the sparse population supports no scene at all. Visitors to smaller towns should expect no visible community infrastructure.

Commentary on Hanovs v. Latvia reads the judgment as a further clarification of the positive obligations of states in homophobic-attack cases: authorities must thoroughly investigate and punish hate crimes to signal zero tolerance. The same analysis places Latvia within a troubling pattern of states in one part of Europe failing to protect LGBTI people and to investigate attacks effectively.
localsOnly:
Adoption rules constrain resident same-sex couples. Latvian law allows any person over 25 to adopt, but persons not married to each other may not adopt the same child, so in an unmarried couple only one partner may adopt. In April 2023 the Saeima amended the Law on the Protection of the Children's Rights to ban adoption of Latvian children by foreign same-sex couples.

Resident same-sex couples have some family-law routes. Lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment, and a 2020 court ruling favouring parental leave rights for same-sex couples fed a Justice Ministry draft civil union law in 2022. The Ombudsman's 2018 call for a partnership law noted that about half of Latvian children are born out of wedlock and should enjoy legal protections.

Workplace discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited since September 2006, when the Saeima passed Labour Code amendments that President Vaira Vīķe-Freiberga refused to sign until that protection was included. The sources record no equivalent protection on the basis of gender identity.

Legal identity change has a contested history. One encyclopaedic account states that surgical gender affirmation and legal identity change are possible in Latvia with a medical certificate required by authorities, and that Latvian law does not define "sex change"; it records a 2004 refusal of identity change to a transgender person after a partial sex change that the Supreme Court overturned in 2008, and a 2009 legislative proposal requiring sterilisation for a legal gender change that the Saeima rejected.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources contradict each other on whether legal gender recognition is available. The June 2025 broadcaster feature and the absence of any cited statute indicate no procedure exists, while an encyclopaedic source states that legal identity change is possible on presentation of a medical certificate and cites a 2008 Supreme Court ruling ordering that a change be granted. No current statute, form or fee schedule for gender marker change is sourced here, and the present practical availability of the route is not verified.

Unresolved: whether the post-judgment reopenings in the Hanovs and Daugavpils matters have produced charges, convictions or sentences is not stated in the inventory. The same is true of the investigation into the former MEP's posts.

Not sourced: no education-specific findings, no data on detention or prison placement for trans detainees, and no documentation of border or visa screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status appear in the inventory. No source addresses whether a foreign visitor's home-country gender marker is recognised for Latvian official purposes.
